query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introduce a controlled, low-level (∼0.5 at%) interstitial nitrogen doping during synthesis to increase the stacking fault energy and improve ductility without perturbing the order–disorder caloric phase transition.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operations but showing poor load-bearing integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Incorporate ∼0.5 at% interstitial N during alloy synthesis by using a reactive atmosphere or alloying precursor adjustment, with process controls (e.g., high-vacuum melting followed by controlled nitrogen backfill) to ensure homogeneous N uptake.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled high-vacuum melting conditions with a precise N partial pressure and subsequent homogenization; testing under typical refrigeration operating regimes (room temperature, applied magnetic/pressure fields).
generation.structural_mediator: Slight increase in stacking fault energy and uniform modification of dislocation dynamics within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial N atoms increase the stacking fault energy, which suppresses excessive nano-twinning or premature crack initiation by promoting more uniform dislocation glide, while maintaining the integrity of the order–disorder transition that produces the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced fracture toughness and ductility (improved load-bearing integrity) while preserving caloric performance within ±10% of the original entropy change and temperature response.
generation.baseline: The undoped (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy that, despite high caloric performance, suffers from poor mechanical integrity and tends to crack.
generation.boundary: Effective within a narrow doping window (around 0.5 at%); higher concentrations risk shifting the phase transition or forming unwanted nitride phases.
generation.uncertainty: Although analogous systems and theoretical models predict non-interference of low-level N doping with caloric behavior, the precise impact in this specific alloy must be validated with pilot microstructural and phase analyses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples via high-vacuum melting: one undoped, one doped with 0.5 at% N, and one with 1.0 at% N. Use in situ synchrotron diffraction and TEM to verify phase stability and stacking fault evolution. Evaluate mechanical properties and measure caloric responses under identical magnetic/pressure field conditions.
measurements: Grain boundary and dislocation analyses via TEM and synchrotron diffraction.
Fracture toughness and tensile strength testing.
Direct measurement of caloric response (entropy change and temperature shift) under controlled field application.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 0.5 at% N-doped sample shows a caloric response reduction exceeding 10% compared to the baseline or no statistically significant improvement in fracture toughness, the hypothesis is falsified.

Our experimental results suggest a volume change of ~10% near Tc at ambient pressure; we estimate PΔV work of ~0.04 meV/unit cell (PΔVwork = Pexternal × ΔV, where Pexternal is the barometric pressure 1 atm, ΔV is the volume change). Thus, the prominent difference in Gibbs free energy between the two phases is dominated by the rotational entropy of NPG molecules. Our previous results show that NPG molecules have many degenerated states during the random rotational process above temperature of phase transition, so it is reasonable to model the molecule as a free 3D rigid rotor in the disordered phase. Here, we present a rapid liquid-phase sintering strategy that improves the densification of high-entropy, high-temperature ceramics without losing their high-entropy structure. We heat the ceramics at temperatures greater than what can be achieved using a conventional furnace or hot pressing (~2500 K), but lower than the ultrahigh temperatures achieved by techniques such as arc melting (~3300 K), which helps to promote effective densification but without completely melting the material, thus preserving the high-entropy structure.

ABSTRACTWe investigated the effects of interstitial N and C on the stacking fault energy (SFE) of an equiatomic CoCrNi medium entropy alloy. Results of computer modeling were compared to tensile deformation and electron microscopy data. Both N and C in solid solution increase the SFE of the face-centered cubic (FCC) alloy matrix at room temperature, with the former having a more significant effect by 240% for 0.5 at % N. Total energy calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) as well as thermodynamic modeling of the Gibbs free energy with the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) method reveal a stabilizing effect of N and C interstitials on the FCC lattice with respect to the hexagonal close-packed (HCP) CoCrNi-X (X: N, C) lattice. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) measurements of the width of dissociated ½<110> dislocations suggest that the SFE of CoCrNi increases from 22 to 42–44 mJ·m−2 after doping the alloy with 0.5 at. % interstitial N.
